quote: The Originall of them all, is that which we call Sense; (For there is no conception in a mans mind, which hath not at first, totally, or by parts, been begotten upon the organs of Sense.)
Singly, they are every one a Representation or Apparence, of some quality, or other Accident of a body without us; which is commonly called an Object.
And this Seeming, or Fancy, is that which men call sense; and consisteth, as to the Eye, in a Light, or Colour Figured.
Imagination therefore is nothing but Decaying Sense; and is found in men, and many other living Creatures, as well sleeping, as waking.
But when we would express the Decay, and signifie that the Sense is fading, old, and past, it is called Memory.
Much memory, or memory of many things, is called Experience.
The imaginations of them that sleep, are those we call Dreams.

The Imagination that is raysed in man (or any other creature indued with the faculty of imagining) by words, or other voluntary signes, is that we generally call Understanding; and is common to Man and Beast.
By Consequence, or Trayne of Thoughts, I understand that succession of one Thought to another, which is called (to distinguish it from Discourse in words) Mentall Discourse.
Which kind of thoughts, is called Foresight, and Prudence, or Providence; and sometimes Wisdome; though such conjecture, through the difficulty of observing all circumstances, be very fallacious.
A Signe, is the Event Antecedent, of the Consequent; and contrarily, the Consequent of the Antecedent, when the like Consequences have been observed, before.
But his conjecture, has the same incertainty almost with the conjecture of the Future; both being grounded onely upon Experience.
chapter_ref: CHAPTER III; Conjecture Of The Time Past

quote: Therefore there is no Idea, or conception of anything we call Infinite.
chapter_ref: CHAPTER III; Conjecture Of The Time Past

quote: The Invention of Printing, though ingenious, compared with the invention of Letters, is no great matter.
But who was the first that found the use of Letters, is not known.
So that the first use of names, is to serve for Markes, or Notes of remembrance.
chapter_ref: CHAPTER IV; The Use Of Speech

quote: Another is, when many use the same words, to signifie (by their connexion and order,) one to another, what they conceive, or think of each matter... and for this use they are called Signes.
chapter_ref: CHAPTER IV; The Use Of Speech

quote: Concerning the Thoughts of man, I will consider them first Singly, and afterwards in Trayne, or dependance upon one another.

By Consequence, or Trayne of Thoughts, I understand that succession of one Thought to another.

One Universall name is imposed on many things, for their similitude in some quality, or other accident.
chapter_ref: CHAPTER IV; Names Proper & Common Universall

quote: there being nothing in the world Universall but Names; for the things named, are every one of them Individual and Singular.

quote: Science is the knowledge of Consequences, and dependance of one fact upon another.
For Reason, in this sense, is nothing but Reckoning (that is, Adding and Substracting) of the Consequences of generall names agreed upon.
And the act of reasoning they called syllogisme; which signifieth summing up of the consequences of one saying to another.
and Many syllogismes to make a Demonstration; and from the Summe, or Conclusion of a syllogisme, they substract one Proposition, to finde the other.
chapter_ref: CHAPTER V; Reason What It Is

quote: if that which he thought likely to follow, followes not... this is called ERROR; to which even the most prudent men are subject.

quote: But when we Reason in Words of generall signification, and fall upon a generall inference which is false... it is indeed an ABSURDITY, or senseless Speech.

quote: The names of such things as affect us... are in the common discourses of men, of Inconstant signification.

quote: or conceive a Remainder, from Substraction of one summe from another.

quote: The Latines called Accounts of mony Rationes, and accounting, Ratiocinatio.
The Greeks have but one word Logos, for both Speech and Reason.
Subject To Names, is whatsoever can enter into, or be considered in an account; and be added one to another to make a summe.
There be also other Names, called Negative; which are notes to signifie that a word is not the name of the thing in question.

quote: Those things which we neither Desire, nor Hate, we are said to Contemne: CONTEMPT being nothing els but an immobility, or contumacy of the Heart.
But whatsoever is the object of any mans Appetite or Desire; that is it, which he for his part calleth Good.
And the object of his Hate, and Aversion, evill; And of his contempt, Vile, and Inconsiderable.
Whereof the former signifies that, which by some apparent signes promiseth Good.

the apparence, or sense of that motion, is that wee either call DELIGHT, or TROUBLE OF MIND.

and the contrary, Molesta, Offensive, from hindering, and troubling the motion vitall.

quote: For Appetite with an opinion of attaining, is called HOPE.
The same, without such opinion, DESPAIRE.
Aversion, with opinion of Hurt from the object, FEARE.
The same, with hope of avoyding that Hurt by resistance, COURAGE.
Sudden Courage, ANGER.

Those that observe their similitudes, in case they be such as are but rarely observed by others, are sayd to have a Good Wit; by which, in this occasion, is meant a Good Fancy.

quote: To Prudence, if you adde the use of unjust, or dishonest means... you have that Crooked Wisdome, which is called CRAFT.
to have stronger, and more vehement Passions for any thing, than is ordinarily seen in others, is that which men call MADNESSE.
Pride, subjecteth a man to Anger, the excesse whereof, is the Madnesse called RAGE, and FURY.
Dejection, subjects a man to causelesse fears; which is a Madnesse commonly called MELANCHOLY.
And that is, when men speak such words, as put together, have in them no signification at all.

quote: The POWER of a Man, (to take it Universally,) is his present means, to obtain some future apparent Good.
The Value, or WORTH of a man, is as of all other things, his Price; that is to say, so much as would be given for the use of his Power.
And as in other things, so in men, not the seller, but the buyer determines the Price.
The publique worth of a man, which is the Value set on him by the Common-wealth, is that which men commonly call DIGNITY.
To Value a man at a high rate, is to Honour him; at a low rate, is to Dishonour him.
To neglect, is to Dishonour... To contemne, or lesse to love or feare then he expects, is to Dishonour.
chapter_ref: CHAPTER X; To Honour and Dishonour

quote: Honourable is whatsoever possession, action, or quality, is an argument and signe of Power.
chapter_ref: CHAPTER X; To Honour and Dishonour

quote: WORTHINESSE, is a thing different from the worth, or value of a man; and also from his merit, or desert; and consisteth in a particular power, or ability for that, whereof he is said to be worthy.
which particular ability, is usually named FITNESSE, or Aptitude.
He that performeth first in the case of a Contract, is said to MERIT that which he is to receive by the performance of the other; and he hath it as Due.
Nature hath made men so equall, in the faculties of body, and mind; as that... the difference between man, and man, is not so considerable.
And from this diffidence of one another, there is no way for any man to secure himselfe, so reasonable, as Anticipation.
during the time men live without a common Power to keep them all in awe, they are in that condition which is called Warre; and such a warre, as is of every man, against every man.

quote: The Passions that encline men to Peace, are Feare of Death; Desire of such things as are necessary to commodious living; and a Hope by their Industry to obtain them.

quote: The RIGHT OF NATURE, which Writers commonly call Jus Naturale, is the Liberty each man hath, to use his own power, as he will himselfe, for the preservation of his own Nature.
chapter_ref: CHAPTER XIV; Right Of Nature What

quote: By LIBERTY, is understood, according to the proper signification of the word, the absence of externall Impediments.
A LAW OF NATURE, (Lex Naturalis,) is a Precept, or generall Rule, found out by Reason, by which a man is forbidden to do, that, which is destructive of his life.
chapter_ref: CHAPTER XIV; A Law Of Nature What

quote: The mutuall transferring of Right, is that which men call CONTRACT.
one of the Contractors, may deliver the Thing contracted for on his part, and leave the other to perform his part at some determinate time after... is called PACT, or COVENANT.
And in this law of Nature, consisteth the Fountain and Originall of JUSTICE. For where no Covenant hath preceded, there hath no Right been transferred.
chapter_ref: CHAPTER XV; The Third Law Of Nature, Justice

quote: It is consequent also to the same condition, that there be no Propriety, no Dominion, no Mine and Thine distinct; but onely that to be every mans that he can get.

quote: The observance of this law, from the equall distribution to each man, of that which in reason belongeth to him, is called EQUITY.

chapter_ref: CHAPTER XV; The Thirteenth, Of Lot

quote: Natural, is either Primogeniture, (which the Greek calls Kleronomia, which signifies, Given by Lot;) or First Seisure.

quote: A PERSON, is he whose words or actions are considered, either as his own, or as representing the words or actions of an other man.

he that oweth his words and actions, is the AUTHOR: In which case the Actor acteth by Authority.
And as the Right of possession, is called Dominion; so the Right of doing any Action, is called AUTHORITY.
